Romans 11:17: you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others.
Galatians 6:16: peace and mercy be upon the Israel of God.
Romans 10:1: my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
Critics reply that whatever it is called, the view still transfers Israel's national promises to the church, and that the term “Israel” in Paul nearly always means ethnic Israel.
Aren't the signs of Matthew 24 being fulfilled today?
Jesus gave the signs to his disciples about their own generation, and history records them before AD 70. Every generation since has found the same signs in its news.

The disciples asked when the temple would be destroyed. Jesus spoke of false christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, the gospel preached to the nations, and the abomination of desolation, and then said this generation would not pass away until all these things took place. Acts and Josephus record false prophets, the famine under Claudius, earthquakes, persecution and the Roman armies around Jerusalem, all within forty years. Wars and earthquakes have happened in every century since, so finding them in today's news proves nothing about today. The study on Matthew 24 goes through every verse.
Acts 11:28: Agabus foretold a great famine, which took place in the days of Claudius.
Colossians 1:23: the gospel has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.
Josephus records false prophets leading crowds into the desert before AD 70.
Futurist readers hold that the signs are “birth pains” that grow in frequency and intensity before the return, so their recurrence today still matters.
Doesn't “as in the days of Noah” mean the world will get more and more wicked?
Jesus' point in Matthew 24:37-39 is that people were unaware: eating, drinking and marrying until the flood came. It is about suddenness, not a rising graph of evil.

Genesis does describe great wickedness before the flood, but Jesus draws a different lesson. He lists ordinary things, eating, drinking, marrying, and says they did not know until the flood came and swept them away. The warning is to be ready because the judgement comes suddenly to people going about normal life. Those “taken” in the comparison are taken by the flood, in judgement. Nothing in the passage says the world must grow steadily worse before Christ comes.
Matthew 24:38-39: eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and they were unaware.
Luke 17:28-30 adds the days of Lot: buying, selling, planting, building.
Matthew 24:42: stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
Many futurists still read the comparison as including the moral state of Noah's world (Genesis 6:5, 11), and see growing violence and corruption as part of the sign.
What about 2 Timothy 3: “in the last days there will come times of difficulty”?
Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people. The “last days” had already come, and Paul adds that the deceivers “will not get very far.”

Paul lists lovers of self, lovers of money, the proud and the abusive, and then says, “avoid such people.” That only makes sense if they were in Timothy's world. The New Testament says the last days began with Christ: God has spoken in these last days by his Son, and Peter called Pentecost the last days of Joel. Verse 9 says the false teachers will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all. Verse 13 says evil people and impostors go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived: that describes the impostors, not the whole world.
2 Timothy 3:5: avoid such people.
Hebrews 1:2: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son.
2 Timothy 3:9: they will not get very far.
Futurist readers agree the last days began at Pentecost, but say they end in a final period when these sins reach a peak.
Does Luke 18:8, “will he find faith on earth?”, mean faith will nearly die out?
The question ends a parable about praying and not losing heart. It challenges the hearers to keep believing; it is not a forecast that the church will shrink.

Jesus told the parable of the widow and the unjust judge to show that his disciples ought always to pray and not lose heart. God will give justice to his elect speedily. Then comes the question, “when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” In context, it presses the hearers: will you keep praying until he vindicates you? The vindication of the persecuted disciples came within their generation. Meanwhile the number of Christians has grown from about 560 million in 1900 to well over two and a half billion.
Luke 18:1: they ought always to pray and not lose heart.
Luke 18:7-8: he will give justice to them speedily.
Christians in Africa grew from about 9 million in 1900 to over 650 million by 2020.
Some futurist readers take the question as a hint of widespread unbelief at the very end; others agree it is a challenge rather than a forecast.
Isn't the great falling away of 2 Thessalonians 2 happening now?
Paul told the Thessalonians the mystery of lawlessness was “already at work” and that they knew what was restraining it. The falling away came in their generation.

Paul wrote to calm believers who thought the day of the Lord had come. First, he said, the rebellion must come and the man of lawlessness be revealed. He reminded them he had told them these things, said they knew what was holding him back, and said the mystery of lawlessness was already at work. Jesus had warned that many would fall away before the end of that age, and the later letters record it: all in Asia turned away from Paul, and John wrote that many antichrists had already come and gone out from the church.
2 Thessalonians 2:5-7: you know what is restraining him; the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.
2 Timothy 1:15: all who are in Asia turned away from me.
1 John 2:18-19: many antichrists have come; they went out from us.
Futurists hold that the rebellion and the man of lawlessness are still future, at the end of the age, and often see today's decline in Western churches as its approach.
Is the world really getting worse?
Some things are worse and much is better. On long-run measures, extreme poverty, child deaths and illiteracy have fallen sharply, and the church has grown more in the last century than in any before.

News reports what goes wrong, and each generation remembers the past as calmer than it was. The long record tells a more mixed story. Around 1800 about four in ten children died before age five; today it is under four in a hundred. Life expectancy has more than doubled. Extreme poverty has fallen from over a third of humanity in 1990 to under a tenth. Real evils remain, and some are new. The Christian claim is not that progress is automatic, but that the risen Christ is ruling, and his kingdom, like yeast, keeps working through the whole loaf.
Child deaths before age five: about 43% around 1800, about 4% today.
Life expectancy: about 29 years in 1800, about 73 today.
Christians worldwide: about 0.56 billion in 1900, about 2.6 billion today.
Premillennial believers answer that material progress is not spiritual progress, that secular Western culture is declining fast, and that Scripture expects evil to ripen before the end.
How has the church grown since the apostles?
From about 120 believers in Acts 1 to around 2.6 billion people who call themselves Christians, with the fastest growth in the last century in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

Acts begins with about 120 disciples. By 300 the church may have numbered several million in the Roman Empire. In 1900 about 558 million people were Christians, most of them in Europe and North America. By 2025 the figure is about 2.6 billion, and the centre has shifted to the global South: Africa alone went from about 9 million Christians in 1900 to over 650 million. That is what the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven describe: small beginnings, great growth.
Acts 1:15: about 120 believers.
Acts 2:41; 4:4: three thousand, then five thousand.
Africa: about 9 million Christians in 1900, over 650 million in 2020.
Some reply that counting nominal Christians overstates true faith, and that numbers do not measure the health of the church.
Are earthquakes increasing, as is often claimed?
No. The US Geological Survey reports roughly the same number of major earthquakes each year over the last century; we simply detect and hear about more of them.

The USGS notes that about fifteen earthquakes of magnitude 7 or greater happen in an average year, and that this rate has stayed fairly constant. There are many more seismograph stations now, so far more small earthquakes are recorded, and news travels instantly. Jesus did mention earthquakes in various places as the beginning of birth pains, and in that generation there were notable ones, including the earthquake at Philippi in Acts 16 and a destructive one at Laodicea around AD 60.
USGS: about 15 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more per year on average.
Acts 16:26: a great earthquake shook the prison at Philippi.
Tacitus records an earthquake that destroyed Laodicea in AD 60.
Some futurists accept that the count is steady but say that the human impact of earthquakes, with larger cities, is greater, or that the sign is not about numbers at all.
Are wars getting worse?
Wars remain terrible, but deaths in battle per head of world population are far below the levels of the two world wars.

Research groups that count battle deaths, such as the Uppsala Conflict Data Program and the Peace Research Institute Oslo, show that the rate of battle deaths per 100,000 people fell steeply after 1945. It rose again with the wars in Ethiopia and Ukraine after 2020, but remains a small fraction of its 20th-century peak. Jesus said, “you will hear of wars and rumours of wars; see that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet.” Wars were never meant as a countdown.
Matthew 24:6: the end is not yet.
In the Second World War, battle deaths ran at over 100 per 100,000 people a year; in most recent years, a few.
AD 66-70 saw civil war in Rome (the year of the four emperors) and the Jewish revolt.
Others warn that nuclear weapons make the risk of a catastrophic war greater than ever, so falling averages give false comfort.
How do I answer a friend who says every prophecy is being fulfilled?
Ask which prophecy and which verse, read it in context with them, look at who it was spoken to and when, and show how many generations have said the same thing.

Start with the text, not the news. Ask: who was this spoken to, and what did it mean to them? Look for time words such as “this generation,” “soon,” “near,” or “some standing here.” Check whether the New Testament already says it was fulfilled. Then look at history: every century has had wars, earthquakes and famines, and every generation of date-setters has been wrong. Finally, point to the promises of a growing kingdom. Do it with humility: your friend loves the Lord and wants to be ready, which is good.
Matthew 16:28: some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
Revelation 1:1, 3: things that must soon take place; the time is near.
Dates set for 1844, 1914, 1988 and 2011 all failed.
Futurists answer that prophecies can have near and far fulfilments, so a first-century fulfilment does not rule out a greater one at the end.
Why does it matter whether we expect the world to get better or worse?
What we expect shapes how we live. A hope that Christ is winning gives courage to evangelise, build, serve and plan for the long term.

If believers expect only decline, it is easy to retreat, to see every problem as a sign, and to fear the news. Scripture gives Christians a different posture: Christ has all authority, he is with us to the end of the age, and the nations will be discipled. The apostles faced far worse than most believers do today, yet they turned the world upside down. Expecting the kingdom to grow does not mean ignoring suffering; it means working against it in Christ's name, confident that our labour in the Lord is not in vain.
Matthew 28:18-20: all authority has been given to me; make disciples of all nations.
1 Corinthians 15:58: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Jeremiah 29:7: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you.
Premillennial believers have also built hospitals, schools and missions, and answer that urgency about Christ's return has itself been a great motive for evangelism.
What does Scripture promise about the growth of Christ's kingdom?
A stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth, a mustard seed that becomes a tree, yeast that leavens all the dough, and a government whose increase will never end.

Daniel saw a stone cut without hands strike the statue of the empires and become a great mountain that filled the whole earth, a kingdom set up in the days of those kings. Jesus compared the kingdom to a mustard seed and to yeast. Isaiah says of the child on David's throne, “of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.” The Psalms promise that all the ends of the earth will turn to the LORD. Paul says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet. These are pictures of steady, unstoppable growth during this age.
Daniel 2:35, 44: the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
Matthew 13:31-33: the mustard seed and the leaven.
Habakkuk 2:14: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.
Amillennial and premillennial believers read these as describing the kingdom's final glory at Christ's return, or its spiritual reach, rather than a visible growth within history.
Doesn't the parable of the wheat and weeds show evil growing with good until the end?
Yes, both grow together until the harvest; the parable does not say the weeds win. In the same chapter, the mustard seed and the leaven describe the kingdom spreading.

Jesus says the field is the world and both wheat and weeds grow until the harvest at the end of the age. That guards against expecting a perfect world before the end, and against trying to root out evil by force. But the parable gives no proportion; it does not say the weeds will take over the field. Matthew sets it beside the mustard seed and the yeast, so the whole chapter teaches both: evil persists, and the kingdom grows.
Matthew 13:30: let both grow together until the harvest.
Matthew 13:31-32: the smallest seed becomes a tree.
Matthew 13:33: until it was all leavened.
Premillennial readers see the parable as the main picture of this age: a mixed field that only Christ's return will put right.

Pandemics like COVID-19 are end-time plagues.
Famine and plague struck that generation (Acts 11:28). Far worse pandemics came long before ours.
